title: Identify and discuss different types of business and their legal implications

lessons.title: Types of business you see around the farm
lessons.html:
Who owns a business?

Every business has an owner. The owner can be one person, a few people, or a group of members. The way the business is set up is called its business type or legal form. The type tells us who makes the decisions, who gets the profit and who must pay if things go wrong.

Sole trader (sole proprietor)

One person owns and runs the business. Think of a man who sells vegetables from his bakkie at the taxi rank, or a woman who runs a small spaza shop near the farm. It is easy and cheap to start. The owner keeps all the profit. But the owner also carries all the risk. If the business owes money, the owner must pay from his or her own pocket.

Partnership

Two or more people own the business together. For example, two brothers rent land and grow cabbages together. They share the work, the money and the profit. They should write down a partnership agreement so everyone knows their share. Each partner can be held responsible for the debts of the partnership.

Company

A company is a business that is registered with the Companies and Intellectual Property Commission (CIPC). In South Africa most small companies are private companies, with (Pty) Ltd after the name. A company is a separate legal person. It can own land, a tractor and a bank account in its own name. The owners are called shareholders.

Co-operative

A co-operative (co-op) is owned by its members, who work together for a shared goal. Many small farmers join a co-op so they can buy seed and fertiliser in bulk at a lower price, or sell their maize or milk together. Each member usually has one vote.

Other forms

Some farms are owned by a family trust. Some community projects are run as a non-profit organisation. Your supervisor can tell you which type of business owns your farm.

lessons.title: What the business type means in law
lessons.html:
Why the legal form matters

The type of business is not just a name. It changes what the law says about the owners. The most important question is: who pays the debts?

TypeWho pays debtsRegistration
Sole traderThe owner, from personal money and goodsNo company registration needed
PartnershipThe partners, from personal moneyWritten agreement is wise
Company (Pty) LtdThe company itself (limited liability)Register with CIPC
Co-operativeThe co-op itselfRegister as a co-operative

Limited and unlimited liability

Unlimited liability means the owner can lose personal things, like a house or car, to pay the business debts. Sole traders and partners have unlimited liability. Limited liability means shareholders can only lose the money they put into the company. Their own houses are protected. This is one big reason people start a company.

Other legal duties

  • Tax: every business must pay tax to SARS on its profit. A sole trader pays tax on the profit as personal income. A company pays company tax.
  • Workers: any business that employs people must follow labour law, for example the Basic Conditions of Employment Act, and register workers for UIF.
  • Records: a company must keep proper records and send yearly returns to CIPC.
  • Licences: some businesses need a trading licence from the municipality.

Example

Thabo sells eggs as a sole trader. A supplier delivers feed and Thabo cannot pay. The supplier can claim from Thabo personally. If Thabo had a registered company, the supplier would claim from the company, not from Thabo's own goods.

Key points

  • A sole trader is one owner; a partnership is two or more owners.
  • A company is registered with CIPC and is a separate legal person.
  • A co-operative is owned by members who work together.
  • Sole traders and partners have unlimited liability; company shareholders have limited liability.
  • Every business must pay tax and follow labour law.
